The backlog, read against the app that exists

The team has a ratified backlog of 19 epics and 102 features. The Prototype section of the project wiki documents every screen the POC app has, 28 of them across 9 named flows, each with its real capture and each capability cited to a line of source. Until now the two had never met. The screen and flow inventory listed per-screen feature extraction as out of scope, and the Prototype section says outright that it generates no backlog items.

This is that pass. For every screen it asks one question, does the backlog cover this, and records the answer with the screen's capture next to the feature it backs. Start on Coverage, which is the cross-reference itself.

19EpicsE00 through E18, every one carried forward
102Features inthe ratified backlog before this pass
25Features addednet-new, marked NEW on their epic tab
3Features retiredremoved on direction, ids not reused
127Features outnothing dropped without a reason
28Screensroute templates in the app's router
9Flowsnamed user journeys, F1 to F9

What this pass is not

It files nothing. No Jira issue is created, edited or transitioned, and the backlog source files are untouched. The features marked NEW here are a proposal for review, and promoting them into tracking/backlog-epics.md is a separate decision. Screens read Covered where an existing feature already does the job, and this pass resisted inventing work to look productive: 10 of 28 screens needed no change at all.

Provenance

Epic and feature text is read at build time from tracking/backlog-epics.md and scripts/data/e00-spikes.json. Band and Jira key come from tracking/epic-board-mapping.md. Screen routes, router files, flow membership and tile filenames are read from the Prototype pages under product/prototype/, which cite the app at c1b3c2d. Tiles are the app's own capture:board output at 72c3ab8, captured 2026-08-31, re-encoded to WebP and inlined so this file works offline from a file:// URL. Every capture is labeled with its source filename, so refreshing a screenshot means dropping in a new PNG and rebuilding.

The screen-to-feature judgement is the one authored input. It lives in scripts/data/screen-backlog-map.json, so it can be argued with directly rather than being buried in a script.

Coverage, every screen against the backlog

One row per route template in the app's router, 28 of them, each with the verdict this pass reached. Covered means an existing feature already describes what the screen does. Extends means a feature covers it partly and the note says what is missing. Gap means nothing in the backlog covered it and this pass proposes a feature. Unmapped means it has no honest home and forcing one would be worse than saying so.

SPRINT 0All lanesSCRIBL-3

E00 Sprint 0, the Shape window

Sprint 0 is the Shape window, 2026-08-24 to 2026-09-01. Seven working days, 20 lane-days, named as a sprint and given a structure it did not have. Sprint 1 keeps its 2026-09-02 start and all four demo dates hold.

Fifteen spikes, each with an owner, a timebox, the question it answers, the artifact it produces, and the sprint 1 work it unblocks. The full table, the per-lane day cost and the not-startable list are in the merged plan below.

Sprint 1 presumes fifteen decisions that nobody has made. A feature-by-feature pass over all 76 features, asking what decision each sprint 1 item presumes, produced six of the fifteen that were on nobody's list.

Fourteen lane-days of the fifteen spikes are new work inside the three build lanes. Green demand was 128 against 108 before Sprint 0 and is 142 against 108 after it. The overrun goes from 20 lane-days to 34. Fourteen lane-days of committed green work have to come out to pay for the spikes, and this page does not choose which.

Six further spike-days sit outside the 108, three on delivery and three on the harness and Arc, so they do not compete with feature work.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

GREENBackend and AWSSCRIBL-1

E01 Cloud foundation and app shell

The board named this first for a reason. Submit-to-unlock is a database precondition and channel isolation is a server-side authorization rule, so both of the product's two hard invariants live in this epic rather than in the app, and neither can be retrofitted without touching every read path. The app shell sits here too, as E01-F9, because it is foundation work with no product surface of its own and it has to exist before any screen in E02 can render.

Grounded in ADR-0002 (serverless-first), ADR-0004 (Aurora Serverless v2 as the operational system of record), ADR-0005 (CDK in TypeScript) and ADR-0007 (submit-to-unlock at the data layer). The multi-region EKS design in docs/context/future-architecture-aws.md is the scale-up target and no part of it is in this epic. Nothing here invents infrastructure the ADRs do not name.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

Doing this before any service exists is what makes the staging environment real: with three demos to Scribl in eight weeks, a demo build has to come off a deployed environment rather than off someone's laptop.

E01-F3Relational data modelBackend
parentE01bandGREENdisciplineBackenddepends onE01-F2blocked bynonestatusNextsize4 backend-dayscarries forwardRE-13

Aurora Serverless v2 with the schema the loop needs: users, channels, memberships, prompts, submissions, the multi-channel share join table, and reactions. ADR-0004 makes Aurora the default and DynamoDB the forward-scale option, and the ADR README still lists the Aurora-versus-DynamoDB choice as a confirm-before-build gate, so the schema work should be written to be portable in its access patterns rather than assuming either engine forever. The join table is not a detail: it is what makes one submission appear on three walls without three copies of the artwork.

E01-F4Serverless API surfaceBackend
parentE01bandGREENdisciplineBackenddepends onE01-F3blocked bynonestatusNextsize5 backend-dayscarries forwardRE-13

API Gateway plus Lambda in TypeScript for the request and response path, per ADR-0002. Endpoints for the loop only: today's prompt, submit, channel read, membership, reactions. The AI service is deliberately not in this path; ADR-0003 puts Claude work in a separate service and ADR-0010 makes it asynchronous, so submit never waits on a model.

E01-F5API contract and mock serverBackend
parentE01bandGREENdisciplineBackenddepends onnoneblocked bynonestatusNextsize2 backend-dayscarries forwardRE-14

A written request and response contract for every endpoint in E01-F4, plus a mock server that answers it. This exists because of the capacity shape rather than because contracts are tidy: with one iOS engineer and one backend engineer, whoever finishes first waits on the other. A mock server means iOS codes against a stub in sprint 1 and QA writes API-level tests before the real API exists. Build it before the endpoints, not after.

One command, or one merge, deploys a CDK stack to an environment. No ADR and no AWS design doc in this repo names a CI tool; ADR-0005 covers infrastructure as code and stops there. Rather than invent one, the starting proposal is Bitbucket Pipelines because the code already lives in Bitbucket (hs2studio/scribl-app), and the tool gets confirmed in discovery. A React Native app with the full route graph reachable, one theme, and error states that never leave a blank screen. One theme, not four: the POC carries four runtime themes and none of them match the client's deck, so the rebuild starts from the deck values (#1D1A34 ink, #D51668 magenta, #F8F8FA surface, Nunito and Prompt) recorded in the POC realignment plan section 1. Three design values are still open and all three are cheap to change later and expensive to change everywhere: the canvas surface color (Q1), whether the splash animates (Q3), and the muted text value (Q4).

Backed by 4 screens, and what each one needs

FEFrontend

ScreenHeader and a bottom nav sit around a date badge, the prompt text, a live countdown tile, and a streak tile, with the primary button's label swapping between Open the canvas and Draw another depending on today's submit status. A bare loading spinner covers the whole body until auth hydration resolves, and a retry control needs to appear if the prompt load fails.

BEBackend
Endpoints
  • GET /prompt/todaygetTodayPrompt()
  • GET /me/statsgetStreak()

Today's prompt and the user's stats for a computed streak both need serving, gated behind an authenticated user so no request fires before auth resolves.

Reads and writes

Pulls auth hydration state, the current user, the prompt store, and the streak store. Bounces to /sign-up once hydration finishes and no user is set, otherwise shows a spinner rather than flashing the prompt; writes nothing on entry or exit, only triggers the two store loads.

QEQuality engineering

Draft cases for QE to review, not final acceptance criteria.

  • happy pathWhen a signed-in person with an unsubmitted day lands on the root route, the prompt, countdown, and streak render with a button reading Open the canvas.
  • edge caseWhen auth hydration has not finished yet, the screen shows only a loading spinner and neither the prompt body nor the sign-up bounce.
  • edge caseWhen hydration finishes with no signed-in user, the screen replaces itself with the sign-up route instead of flashing the prompt.

Screen page, product/prototype/screens/root-today.md

FEFrontend

A themed ghost icon, a heading, one line of body copy, and a single Back to Today button, laid out as a small centered card with no header chrome or nav bar.

BEBackend

GREENiOS and BackendSCRIBL-27

E02 Auth and onboarding

An account, and the first two minutes that decide whether someone comes back tomorrow. The client's own Figma flow is better than the POC's here and the difference is worth naming: theirs opens on a personalized invite ("Matthew has invited you to their Family wall", "Hi Sarah"), walks a guided first drawing, and lands that drawing on the inviter's wall. The POC shows a static three-panel tutorial. Teaching by doing and paying off the social loop inside the first minute is the whole product, so this epic adopts their flow rather than restyling ours.

Federation is out. The plan of record is backend-managed email and password on a Cognito user pool, no Apple or Google sign-in, with federation left to a later phase (T4 in the rebuild dataset, ADR-0001 for the secure token seam).

9 of these features are net-new from this pass. Everything else is the backlog as it stands.

15 features

Recommended as a Cognito user pool with email and password only, so nobody in this team writes password storage. The POC stubbed this and the rebuild cannot: every other feature's authorization checks read the identity this feature issues.

GREENBackend and iOSSCRIBL-34

E03 Daily prompt

One prompt a day, the same for everyone, that the app can never edit. Everything else in the product hangs off it, which is why a day without a prompt is an outage rather than a bug.

The board's own wording needs a note. The board sticky says "Daily prompt (Claude)". The kickoff two hours earlier decided the opposite: prompts stay curated by Scribl's program team of mental-health professionals and educators, with Claude scoped to drafting suggestions for their review, because Eric Rice's words were "our entire modality is based on these prompts and making sure that we have final say and a hand in them". No runtime prompt-generation pipeline was ever built. Prompts have always been an admin-curated set, seeded into the database and resolved by date. The pipeline that was built and then disabled is the AI background enhancement, behind the EXPO_PUBLIC_AI_ENABLED flag and off by default, which is what the walkthrough names at 00:47:45. So the board sticky and the client decision disagree, and the client decision wins. This epic ships a seeded curated set on the same fetch contract runtime generation would use later, plus a Claude drafting tool the client's editors operate. Nobody should read the board sticky as authorization to generate prompts at runtime.

4 of these features are net-new from this pass. Everything else is the backlog as it stands.

9 features

E03-F1Seeded prompt set and fetch contractBackend
parentE03bandGREENdisciplineBackenddepends onE01-F3, E01-F4blocked bynonestatusNextsize2 backend-dayscarries forwardRE-03

A curated set loaded into the database, one prompt resolved per calendar day per timezone, served on a contract that does not change if generation ever moves server-side. A rotating fallback so a scheduling failure never leaves a day blank. The contract is the deliverable here as much as the data is.

GREENiOS and BackendSCRIBL-40

E04 Drawing and submit, with submit-to-unlock

The thing people actually do. Draw with a deliberately small set of tools, add a story in text, submit, and only then get to see what anyone else made. The constraint is the feature: six inks and one brush means nobody opens the app and feels unqualified, and the client's own frames are stricter than our POC was.

Submit-to-unlock is not UI. ADR-0007 puts it at the data layer as a transactional existence check on (user, prompt), returning 403 on a channel read until a submission row exists, precisely so no client bug and no direct API call can bypass it. Treat a bypass as a defect of the same severity as a privacy leak.

4 of these features are net-new from this pass. Everything else is the backlog as it stands.

10 features

E04-F1Skia canvas with one brush and the client's eight colorsiOS
parentE04bandGREENdisciplineiOSdepends onE01-F9blocked bynonestatusNextsize5 iOS-dayscarries forwardRE-04

React Native Skia canvas (ADR-0006). The tool set is the client's decision and this is it: one brush at a single weight, eight colors, undo, erase, and a trash control for a clean slate. No brush-size row, no fill tool, no brush styles, no layers.

The eight colors, in the order the client gave them, which is deliberately not ROYGBIV: #db0632 red, #f58c29 orange, #ffd93b yellow, #afd129 light green, #1d864a dark green, #99d9d9 light blue, #20145f dark blue, #d51668 magenta. The last one is the brand magenta exactly. Erase carries the same weight as the brush and reads equally well as a white color option, which is how the POC renders it.

Per-wall narrowing of this palette is data, not a code path, through allowedColors. That is the seam E18 keeps.

Two things are still open and neither blocks building the screen. The drawing area wants a more defined bounding box, possibly a function of the background. And the final on-screen layout and order of the eight swatches is unsettled, possibly primary colors ahead of secondary.

How this spec was settled, including the earlier four-sizes-and-six-inks frame it replaced, is in knowledge/client-feedback/2026-08-25-eric-screen-feedback.md and the change-request record. It is history and does not belong in the story.

E04-F2Stroke serialization and artwork captureiOS
parentE04bandGREENdisciplineiOSdepends onE04-F1blocked bynonestatusNextsize2 iOS-dayscarries forwardRE-04

Strokes stored as vectors, plus a raster capture for the wall grid. Storing strokes rather than only pixels is what makes drawing playback possible later without re-recording anything, and no raster-only competitor can retrofit it. It costs almost nothing to do now and cannot be added retroactively to art already submitted.

GREENiOS and BackendSCRIBL-47

E05 Walls and channels

Private walls that feel like a family fridge instead of a feed. Invitation only, no discovery, no strangers, no followers, and a response posted to the Family wall is invisible from the Friends wall. That isolation is enforced server-side by membership on the channel id, and a leak between two channels is a privacy incident rather than a display bug, which is why its regression test is a launch gate.

7 of these features are net-new from this pass. Everything else is the backlog as it stands.

13 features

parentE05bandGREENdisciplineBackenddepends onE01-F3blocked byQ29statusBlockedsize3 backend-dayscarries forwardRE-07

Channels with members, roles and an invitation-only join path, reusing the resolve-or-create invitee pattern the POC already proved. How many fixed channels ship, three or four, and whether coworkers is its own channel, is still open (Q29). The schema does not care about the number; the onboarding copy, the share-to checklist and the dashboard list all do, so the answer is needed before E02-F4 is built rather than after.

GREENQASCRIBL-54

E06 QA foundation and standards

The 2026-08-20 walkthrough named the problem. QA starts on day one and there is no code, so there is nothing to write test cases against until week three at the earliest. The sequence agreed on that call is the right one: documented and reviewed requirements first, then test cases generated from those requirements plus the design frames, because a mockup does not tell you what the screen was meant to achieve.

So this epic is the standard rather than the suite. What process this team runs, what tooling it uses and why, what the alternatives were, what the coverage commitment actually is, and all of it written up and agreed with Scribl. Three things make it substantial enough to fill two discovery weeks and a first sprint rather than being a warm-up. Scribl has no test automation framework and expects the recommendation to come from Bounteous (Q58). The real-device versus simulator versus hosted-farm choice is also ours, and a subscription needs a case for a specific product before Scribl takes it on (Q59). And the coverage bar is genuinely undecided: the 2026-08-20 walkthrough surfaced three candidate bars, from a full suite plus end-to-end automation, to 80 percent unit coverage, to a deliberately light foundation that keeps the eight weeks on product (Q48). That is the largest open sizing question on the engagement and this epic is where it gets settled.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

7 features

E06-F1QA process standard for this engagementQA
parentE06bandGREENdisciplineQAdepends onnoneblocked bynonestatusNowsize3 QA-dayscarries forwardRE-14

The written process: how a feature moves from ready to tested, what evidence counts, who signs off, and what happens when a build fails a gate. Sized to three two-week sprints and a remote team split across Central and IST rather than to a general-purpose QA handbook. Client-facing document, because it is the reference both sides work from when a build is called tested.

E06-F2Tooling recommendation with the alternatives written downQA
parentE06bandGREENdisciplineQAdepends onnoneblocked byQ53, Q58, Q59statusNowsize4 QA-dayscarries forwardRE-14

Three recommendations, each with the options considered and the reason for the call: the automation framework for a React Native app on iOS, the device strategy (real devices, simulators or a hosted farm), and where test cases live given that nobody knows yet whether the Bounteous Jira instance does test-case management (Q53). Write the cost of each option next to it, because the subscription question needs a case before it can be approved.

E06-F3Test strategy and a priced coverage commitmentQA
parentE06bandGREENdisciplineQAdepends onE06-F2blocked byQ48statusBlockedsize3 QA-dayscarries forwardRE-14

What gets unit tested, what gets automated end to end, what stays manual, and what the number is, with the cost of each layer in QA-days against the 30 QA-days this engagement actually has. An 80 percent unit coverage commitment across three two-week sprints is a different engagement from a manual-plus-smoke commitment, and the difference lands on the iOS lane, which has no slack. Settle the number with Scribl before it gets quoted anywhere else.

E06-F4Requirements review and traceabilityQA
parentE06bandGREENdisciplineQAdepends onE06-F1blocked byQ15, Q16statusNowsize4 QA-dayscarries forwardRE-14

E10 Moderation, fail-safe

The walls are private and invitation-only, which lowers the risk but does not remove it, and App Store review does not grade on intent. Any app with user-generated content needs report, block and takedown before it reaches the public store, and the board's own word for this item is fail-safe, meaning content is held rather than published when moderation cannot reach a verdict. That policy call is not made yet and it is not ours to make alone: the ADR review left fail-open versus fail-safe per content type as an open gate, and the kickoff deferred the depth of content-safety tooling beyond a written point of view for phase one (Q31).

E12 Sharing a response, and a wall, as a document

The orange band carried a sticky reading "Sharing personal" with no epic behind it. This is that epic. Today a drawing goes onto a wall and stays there: the only way to get it out is a screenshot, which loses the story written underneath it and loses the prompt that produced it.

The scope is one picture. Pick a response, and get a file that carries the artwork with its story underneath, ready to send anywhere, including social. That is the whole of the orange work.

Picking several and grouping them into one file is the same idea extended, and it is the gray sticky on the board rather than the orange one. It is E12-F2, deferred, because a multi-page composition is a different rendering job from a single-page one and may need work this epic has not sized.

The format is not decided. A PDF travels everywhere, prints, and needs no hosting. A single HTML file keeps the type and the layout closer to the app and can hold more than one page cheaply. Pick one in scoping rather than building both.

This epic touches the product's privacy promise, so it does not get built without the question in E12-F5 answered first. Walls are private and invitation-only. A shareable file is by definition a copy that leaves that boundary.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

5 features

E12-F1Share one response as a documentBackend
parentE12bandORANGEdisciplineBackenddepends onE04-F4, E01-F6blocked byformat decision, E12-F5statusNewsizenot sized

One response in, one document out: the artwork at print resolution, the story text underneath it, the prompt it answered, and the date. Rendered server-side from the stored submission rather than screenshotted on the device, so the output is the same whatever phone it came from.

Rendering on the server rather than the client is the decision worth making early. The device has the artwork on screen and could compose the file itself, which is cheaper to build and impossible to change later without shipping an app update. The server has the originals in S3 already.

E13 Comments, with the wall creator as moderator

The kickoff settled that reactions ship and open commenting waits, and that if commenting is built it is a switch the wall's creator holds rather than a feature that is always on. This epic is that design, written down.

The part that makes it Scribl's rather than generic is who moderates. The person who made the wall moderates the wall. A parent who creates a family wall gets the hide, the delete and the remove-member action on their own wall, and does not wait on Scribl support to use them. That is a smaller and more defensible surface than central moderation, and it is the reason commenting can be considered at all on a product holding children's work.

The AI filter in E13-F5 sits in front of publication, not behind it: text is checked before anyone sees it. Its fail policy is the same open question E10 and E00-F13 already carry, so it gets answered once for both.

The board had this sticky in the gray band, outside the eight weeks. This session moved it up, so the epic is written to be plannable rather than parked. Its band is a decision, not an inheritance.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

E13-F1Comment model and the per-wall switchBackend
parentE13bandORANGEdisciplineBackenddepends onE01-F3, E05-F1blocked bynonestatusNewsizenot sized

Comments against a response, and a per-wall setting, default off, that only the wall's creator can change. Off means the endpoints refuse rather than the client hiding a button, in the same way submit-to-unlock is enforced at the data layer in E01-F3 rather than in the app.

Default off is the point. A wall that gains a comment box because Scribl shipped an update is a wall whose creator did not agree to it.

Flat, not threaded. Threads are a moderation surface, and the whole shape of this epic is keeping the moderation surface small enough for one parent to manage.

Hide a comment, delete a comment, mute a member on this wall, remove a member from this wall. Authorized against wall creator rather than against a global role, and enforced server-side on the same isolation rule as E05-F2.

Every action is recorded. A moderation action nobody can see the history of is a moderation action the creator cannot explain to the family member on the other end of it.

parentE13bandORANGEdisciplineBackenddepends onE13-F1, E10-F1blocked bynonestatusNewsizenot sized

A member reports a comment to the wall creator, and anything the creator cannot or will not resolve escalates into the moderation lane E10 already builds. App Store review expects a report path for user-generated content and does not accept the wall creator as the only recourse.

This is the seam between creator moderation and Scribl moderation. Draw it here rather than discovering it during review.

E13-F5Pre-publish safety check on comment textBackend
parentE13bandORANGEdisciplineBackenddepends onE13-F1, E10-F1blocked bythe moderation fail policy, E00-F13statusBlocked on the fail policysizenot sized

A comment is checked before it is published, not after it is seen: is it harmful, is it cruel, does it fail the standard Scribl sets. Held rather than shown when the check cannot reach a verdict, which is what the board's own word "fail-safe" means.

The standard itself is Scribl's to write, not the build team's to infer. Their program team owns the language for prompts and it should own the language for this. What engineering owns is the seam and the behaviour on failure.

Note the cost shape. Every comment is a model call, so this is the second place after E03 where AI spend scales with usage rather than with the team, and E08-F4 is where that shows up.

Public submission, not distribution. E16 Under-13 and the COPPA Family edition

Children are the obvious audience for a family drawing app and they are also the one audience that changes the legal shape of the product. COPPA compliance is not a feature you add; it changes consent, data retention, moderation posture and the age rating on the store listing. The board put it after launch planning and that is right, with one caveat: shipping to the public store without an age gate, and then adding an under-13 edition later, may be a harder path than deciding the position before the first submission. Whether Apple's parental-approval flow mitigates the requirement is an open question tracked as Q32.

E17 Monetization

Gray on the board, and it had no epic. The kickoff was clear on the shape of it: not freemium forever, and the paywall hooks belong in the infrastructure for the store release even if nothing is switched on at launch. Nothing in the backlog builds those hooks, so the release-day decision currently has no code behind it.

What is actually sold is not decided, and one earlier assumption behind it no longer holds. The direction was upgraded expression, more inks and more brushes than the free tier gives, resting on a fuller tool set already built and parked. That parked tool set was retired on 2026-09-01: the client chose the tools and the eight colors the app ships with and that choice is final, so there is no richer set sitting behind a flag for a paid tier to unlock.

What survives is the mechanism, not the merchandise. Allowed brushes and colors are per-wall data rather than compiled-in, so a paid tier can read that seam instead of anyone adding a second one. But somebody has to decide what a paid tier would actually contain now that "more tools" is not sitting there ready. E17-F1 is where that lands.

Deciding what is behind the paywall is the first feature here, and it is a product decision with a safeguard attached: whatever is sold, the daily loop that makes the product worth opening has to stay free.

Nothing added to this epic by this pass.

E18 Parked capability

The new designs made the app simpler. This epic holds what the POC built and the product then set aside, so the simplification is recorded as what it actually is, a reduction in surface rather than a deletion of code.

Two things are parked here now, voice notes and Artifacts. Three others were retired on 2026-09-01, and the reasons are below. One mechanism from the retired work is worth keeping, the per-wall restriction seam, allowedBrushStyles and allowedColors as data. That seam is how E04-F1's palette is expressed today, and it is what a future wall type would use to ask for different tools. It earns its place on its own rather than as the door to a parked tool set.

Where each re-enters. Voice notes re-enter the moment the client reconciles their own frames with their own board decision (Q18). Artifacts re-enter with Beta, where key decision 6 parked them (Q19).

Retired on 2026-09-01. Three features left this epic on Rob's direction. They are recorded here rather than deleted quietly, because a feature that vanishes with no trace reads later as an oversight. The three ids are retired rather than reused, so a later feature under E18 takes the next free number instead of stepping into a vacated one.

E18-F1 Full drawing tool set behind the flag. The feature specified four brush styles, sixteen colors, six sizes and a fill tool behind EXPO_PUBLIC_FULL_TOOLSET. No such tool set was ever decided. The client chose the tools and the colors the app ships with and that choice is final, so there is no richer set parked behind a flag waiting to be turned on. What is real, and what stays, is the per-wall restriction seam, allowedColors and allowedBrushStyles as data. E04-F1 now carries the client's decision outright instead of describing it as a reduction from a fuller set.

E18-F2 Challenges. The capability arrived instead as prompt packs plus a wall creator's own prompt, which is what C15 asked for when it recorded "for the time being, we'll just trim it down to prompt injection" and said this feature needed splitting. The prompt-pack half shipped in the POC and is filed as its own features under E03. Nothing is left parked. The blind draw-off, the server-enforced blindness and the leaderboard were the parts the product dropped.

E18-F5 AI enhancement pipeline. Built in the POC, disabled at Scribl's request, and never turned back on. It is not parked pending a decision, the decision was taken. One structural property is worth remembering if it ever returns: drawing bytes never reached an image model, only the Claude-produced caption crossed that seam.

1 of these features are net-new from this pass. Everything else is the backlog as it stands.
